title: Present Simple - affirmative sentences
shortExplanation: I work. He works. She goes. It runs.
longExplanation:
Present Simple is used for: habits and regular actions, facts and general truths, schedules.
Formula: I/you/we/they + infinitive; he/she/it + infinitive+s/es
Rules for writing endings -s/-es:
• Most verbs: + s → works, plays
• Ending in -o, -ch, -sh, -s, -ss, -x: + es → goes, watches, washes
• End with a consonant + -y: -y → ies → studies, tries
formation: I work. He works. She goes. It runs.

title: Stative verbs - verbs not used in Continuous
shortExplanation: I know, not: I am knowing. I love, not: I am loving.
longExplanation:
Some verbs describe a state rather than an action - they are not used in Continuous tenses.
Main groups:
• Opinions: know, believe, think, understand, remember, forget
• Feelings: love, hate, like, want, need, prefer
• Perception: see, hear, smell, taste, look
• Being: be, exist, belong, contain, seem, appear
formation: I know, not: I am knowing. I love, not: I am loving.

Possessive adjectives show ownership and go before the noun.
Important: its (without apostrophe) = ownership; it's (with an apostrophe) = it is.
Do not change in gender and number: my friend / my friends - the same.

shortExplanation: There is a park. There are five rooms.
longExplanation:

shortExplanation: in the box, on the table, at the station
longExplanation:
Three main prepositions:
• in = inside something: in the box, in the city, in bed
• on = on the surface: on the table, on the wall, on the left
• at = at a specific point: at the station, at home, at school
Others: under (under), next to/beside (near), behind (behind), in front of (in front), between (between), opposite (opposite)

Negation: Don't + infinitive

• what = what/which
• where = where/where
• who = who (question without do: Who lives here?)
• when = when
• why = why
• how = how; how much = how many (uncountable); how many = how many (count); how old = how old; how long = how long

Tens: twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety.

• Singular: Tom's book, the dog's tail
• Plural with -s: apostrophe only: the teachers' room, my parents' house
• Irregular plural: 's: the children's playground, men's clothes

• along = along: walk along the river
• across = across/through: swim across the lake, walk across the road

Past Simple - a completed action in the past with or without a specific tense.
Rules for writing the ending -ed:
• Most verbs: + ed → worked, played
• End in -e: + d → loved, used
• Consonant + -y: -y → ied → studied, tried
• One vowel + one consonant (short stressed syllable): double the consonant → stopped, planned

title: Past Simple - irregular verbs (table)
shortExplanation: go→went, see→saw, have→had, come→came, buy→bought
longExplanation:
About 200 irregular verbs need to be learned by heart. The most frequent 50 cover ~90% of uses.
Groups by similarity of changes:
• AAA (do not change): cut, put, hit, set, let
• ABA (return to the beginning): run→ran→run, come→came→come
• ABC (all different): go→went→gone, be→was/were→been
formation: go→went, see→saw, have→had, come→came, buy→bought

shortExplanation: I'll call you back. It will rain tomorrow. I'll have the pasta.

will is used for:
1. Spontaneous decisions (made at the time of speech): I'll help you with that.
2. Predictions without a specific plan: I think it will rain.
3. Promises: I won't tell anyone.
4. Requests: Will you open the window?

Form: am/is/are + verb + -ing

• Most: just + ing → working, playing
• Ends with -e: remove -e + ing → making, coming
• Short stressed syllable: double the last consonant → running, sitting

• I'll meet Alice tomorrow - intention or proposal

mustn't - a strict prohibition (absolutely impossible!).

longExplanation:
Countable: you can count, there are plural. number: a book, two books.
Uncountable: cannot be counted directly - no plural. numbers, no indefinite article.
Typical uncountables: water, milk, bread, rice, money, information, advice, news, weather, luggage, furniture, hair, music, work
To indicate portions: a glass of water, a piece of advice, a loaf of bread, a bag of rice
formation: water, information, advice - not allowed: a water, two advices

examples.translation: May I know something?

examples.sentence: She gave me very useful advice.
examples.translation: She gave me very useful advice.

pattern: Prepositions in / on / at for time
title: Prepositions in / on / at for time
shortExplanation: in March, in 2024, in winter; on Monday, on June 5; at 3pm, at night
longExplanation:
at → exact time: at 6 o'clock, at noon, at midnight, at night, at the weekend (BrE)
on → days and dates: on Monday, on 5 March, on my birthday, on New Year's Day
in → periods: in July, in 2023, in the morning/afternoon/evening, in summer, in the 21st century
Without preposition: this/last/next + time: this morning, last week, next year
formation: in March, in 2024, in winter; on Monday, on June 5; at 3pm, at night

examples.sentence: The meeting is at half past three.
examples.translation: Meeting at half past four.

examples.sentence: She was born on the 12th of April.
examples.translation: She was born on April 12.

examples.sentence: I started this job in October.
examples.translation: I started this work in October.

title: for / since / ago - duration and beginning
shortExplanation: for three years, since 2020, three years ago
longExplanation:
for - duration (how long): for two hours, for a week, for years. Used with different tenses.
since - initial moment (since): since Monday, since 2019, since I was a child. Used with the Present Perfect.
ago - time ago from now: three days ago, a month ago. Only with Past Simple.
formation: for three years, since 2020, three years ago

examples.sentence: I've been here for six months.

examples.sentence: She's worked here since 2020.
examples.translation: She has been working here since 2020.

examples.translation: I saw him two days ago.

title: Tail questions: ...isn't it? / ...do you? / ...haven't they?
shortExplanation: It's cold, isn't it? You like jazz, don't you?
longExplanation:
Tag questions are used to confirm or clarify.
Rule: affirmative sentence → negative tag, and vice versa.
Auxiliary verb in the tail = tense of the main sentence.
Intonation: ↘ (falling) = confirmation; ↗ (rising) = real question.
formation: It's cold, isn't it? You like jazz, don't you?

examples.sentence: It's a nice day, isn't it?
examples.translation: Nice day, right?

examples.sentence: You don't like horror films, do you?
examples.translation: You don't like horror films, do you?

examples.sentence: She can swim, can't she?
examples.translation: She can swim, can't she?

title: have got - possession (British version)
shortExplanation: I've got a car. Have you got a pen? She hasn't got time.
longExplanation:
have got is a colloquial British form of possession. Value = have.
• Affirmation: I have got / I've got a laptop.
• Denial: I haven't got / I don't have
• Question: Have you got...? / Do you have...?
formation: I've got a car. Have you got a pen? She hasn't got time.

examples.sentence: I've got two brothers.
examples.translation: I have two brothers.

examples.sentence: Have you got the time?
examples.translation: Don't you know what time it is?

examples.sentence: She hasn't got any cash.
examples.translation: She doesn't have cash.

title: Adverbs of manner: quickly, carefully, well, hard, fast
shortExplanation: She sings beautifully. He works hard. She drives fast.
longExplanation:
Most adverbs are formed from adjectives + -ly: quick → quickly, careful → carefully, slow → slowly.
Special cases:
• good → well (not goodly)
• fast → fast (not fastly)
• hard → hard (not hardly - this is another word: “barely”)
• late → late (not lately - this is “lately”)
Place: usually after the verb/object: She speaks English well.
formation: She sings beautifully. He works hard. She drives fast.

examples.sentence: He explained it clearly.
examples.translation: He explained it clearly.

examples.sentence: She ran fast.
examples.translation: She ran fast.

examples.sentence: They worked hard all day.
examples.translation: They worked hard all day.

pattern: Adverbs of frequency and their place in a sentence
title: Adverbs of frequency and their place in a sentence
shortExplanation: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never - before the main verb
longExplanation:
Adverbs of frequency: always, usually, often, sometimes, occasionally, rarely, rarely, never.
Place in a sentence:
• Before the main verb: She always drinks tea.
• After the verb to be: He is always late.
• After the auxiliary verb: She has never been to Italy.
Also: every day/week, once a week, twice a month - at the end of the sentence.
formation: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never - before the main verb

examples.sentence: I usually wake up at 7.
examples.translation: I usually wake up at 7.

examples.sentence: She is never late for work.
examples.translation: She is never late for work.

examples.sentence: They meet once a week.
examples.translation: They meet once a week.

title: Order of adjectives before nouns
shortExplanation: a lovely small old red Italian leather bag
longExplanation:
When several adjectives appear before a noun, a strict order is observed: Opinion → Size → Age → Shape → Color → Origin → Material → Purpose
(Opinion → Size → Age → Shape → Color → Origin → Material → Purpose)
Example: a small beautiful old square brown French wooden writing desk
formation: a lovely small old red Italian leather bag

examples.sentence: a lovely little old cottage
examples.translation: lovely little old cottage

examples.sentence: a big red Italian sports car
examples.translation: big red italian sports car

title: Present Perfect - form and meaning
shortExplanation: I have seen it. She has gone. They have arrived.
longExplanation:
Present Perfect = have/has + V3 (third form of the verb).
Three main meanings:
1. Life Experience (no time specified): I have visited Tokyo.
2. Result in the present: I have lost my keys. (there are no keys now)
3. Unfinished action, ongoing now: She has lived here for 5 years.
V3 regular verbs = Past Simple (worked, played). Incorrect ones need to be known separately.
formation: I have seen it. She has gone. They have arrived.

examples.sentence: Have you ever eaten sushi?
examples.translation: Have you ever eaten sushi?

examples.sentence: I've just finished my homework.
examples.translation: I just finished my homework.

examples.sentence: She hasn't called yet.
examples.translation: She hasn't called yet.

title: ever / never / already / yet / just - Present Perfect markers
shortExplanation: Have you ever...? I've never... I've already... Not yet. I've just...
longExplanation:
ever - someday (in questions about experience). Location: in front of V3.
never - never (negative value). Location: in front of V3.
already - already (earlier than expected). Place: before V3 or at the end.
yet - already/yet. In questions (Have you finished yet?) and negations (I haven't finished yet). Place: end of sentence.
just - just now. Location: in front of V3.
formation: Have you ever...? I've never... I've already... Not yet. I've just...

examples.sentence: Have you ever been to Scotland?
examples.translation: Have you been to Scotland?

examples.sentence: I've never eaten snails.
examples.translation: I've never eaten snails.

examples.sentence: I've already seen that film.
examples.translation: I've already seen this film.

title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple - the key difference
shortExplanation: I've been to Paris (experience) vs I went to Paris in 2019 (specific time)
longExplanation:
This is one of the most important differences in English grammar.
Present Perfect - connection with the present, time is NOT indicated:
I've lost my wallet. (no wallet now - this is important)
Past Simple - completed past, time is indicated or implied:
I lost my wallet yesterday. (yesterday is a specific time)
formation: I've been to Paris (experience) vs I went to Paris in 2019 (specific time)

examples.sentence: I've met the new director.
examples.translation: I met the new director.

examples.sentence: I met him last Tuesday.
examples.translation: I met him last Tuesday.

pattern: Present Perfect with for and since
title: Present Perfect with for and since
shortExplanation: I've lived here for 5 years / since 2019.
longExplanation:
for - duration: for two days, for a year, for a long time, for ages
since - starting point: since Monday, since I was a child, since 2015
The question “How long?” — How long + Present Perfect: How long have you known her?
formation: I've lived here for 5 years / since 2019.

examples.sentence: She's worked here for ten years.
examples.translation: She's been working here for ten years.

examples.sentence: I've known him since university.
examples.translation: I've known him since university.

title: Present Perfect Continuous: have been + V-ing
shortExplanation: I have been waiting for an hour. She has been studying all day.
longExplanation:
Present Perfect Continuous = have/has been + V-ing
Emphasis on duration or incompleteness of action. Answers the question “How long?”
Often explains the visible result in the present: You look tired - have you been running?
Difference with Present Perfect Simple:
• I've read 50 pages. - result, completeness
• I've been reading all evening. - emphasis on the process
formation: I have been waiting for an hour. She has been studying all day.

examples.sentence: I've been learning English for two years.
examples.translation: I've been learning English for two years now.

examples.sentence: Why are your hands dirty? — I've been fixing the car.
examples.translation: Why are your hands dirty? — I was repairing the car.

title: Past Continuous: was/were + V-ing
shortExplanation: I was reading at 8pm. They were talking all evening.
longExplanation:
Past Continuous = was/were + V-ing
Values:
1. Action in process at a specific moment in the past: At 9pm I was having dinner.
2. Background activity interrupted by another: I was walking when it started to rain.
3. Parallel actions: While she was cooking, he was watching TV.
formation: I was reading at 8pm. They were talking all evening.

examples.sentence: It was raining when I left home.
examples.translation: It was raining when I left the house.

examples.sentence: What were you doing at 7 yesterday?
examples.translation: What were you doing yesterday at 7?

title: Past Simple vs Past Continuous - background and event
shortExplanation: While I was cooking, he called. I was walking when it started to rain.
longExplanation:
Typical design: long background action (Past Continuous) + short event (Past Simple).
Unions:
• when - used with the Past Simple for the event: She was sleeping when the alarm went off.
• while/as - used with Past Continuous for background: While I was watching TV, the power went out.
formation: While I was cooking, he called. I was walking when it started to rain.

examples.sentence: She was having a bath when the phone rang.
examples.translation: She was taking a bath when the phone rang.

examples.sentence: While he was giving his speech, someone fell asleep.
examples.translation: While he was making his speech, someone fell asleep.

title: Type 0: If + Present, Present - facts and laws
shortExplanation: If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.
longExplanation:
Type zero - for scientific facts, laws of nature, general truths. Both actions always happen together.
Form: If + Present Simple, Present Simple
Instead of if you can use when: When you mix red and blue, you get purple.
formation: If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.

examples.sentence: If you heat ice, it melts.
examples.translation: If you heat ice, it melts.

examples.sentence: If it rains, the streets get wet.
examples.translation: If it rains, the streets get wet.

title: 1st type: If + Present Simple, will - real future
shortExplanation: If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay home.
longExplanation:
A real, probable situation in the future.
Form: If + Present Simple, will + infinitive
Instead of will in the main part you can: can, may, might, should.
Parts can be changed: I'll stay home if it rains. (without comma)
formation: If it rains tomorrow, I'll stay home.

examples.sentence: If she studies hard, she'll pass the exam.
examples.translation: If she studies well, she will pass the exam.

examples.sentence: If you need help, I can come.
examples.translation: If you need help, I can come.

title: Type 2: If + Past Simple, would - unreal present
shortExplanation: If I had a car, I would drive to work. If I were you...
longExplanation:
An unreal or unlikely situation in the present or future.
Form: If + Past Simple, would + infinitive
formation: If I had a car, I would drive to work. If I were you...

examples.sentence: If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.
examples.translation: If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.

examples.sentence: If I were taller, I'd play basketball.
examples.translation: If I were taller, I would play basketball.

title: Type 1 vs Type 2: real vs unlikely
shortExplanation: If I win (1st, really) vs If I won (2nd, unlikely)
longExplanation:
The choice of type reflectsyour confidencein the reality of the situation.
• If I see her (1st type) - I expect to see her
• If I saw her (2nd type) - unlikely or I’m just fantasizing
This is not a difference in grammar, but a difference in the attitude of the speaker.
formation: If I win (1st, really) vs If I won (2nd, unlikely)

examples.sentence: If it rains tomorrow, I'll take an umbrella.
examples.translation: If it rains tomorrow, I will take an umbrella.

examples.sentence: If it rained every day, I'd move to Spain.
examples.translation: If it rained every day, I would move to Spain.

title: Passive Voice - Present Simple: is/are + V3
shortExplanation: Coffee is grown in Brazil. The car is made in Germany.
longExplanation:
Passive voice is used when:
• The action itself is important, not the person who performs it
• Performer unknown or obvious
Form Present Simple Passive: am/is/are + V3
The performer (if needed) is added with by: The window was broken by the ball.
formation: Coffee is grown in Brazil. The car is made in Germany.

examples.sentence: English is spoken in many countries.
examples.translation: English is spoken in many countries.

examples.sentence: The letter is written in French.
examples.translation: The letter is written in French.

title: Passive Voice - Past Simple: was/were + V3
shortExplanation: The bridge was built in 1890. They were arrested.
longExplanation:
Past Simple Passive: was/were + V3
• was - units. number
• were - plural. number
Active → Passive: Someone stole my car. → My car was stolen.
formation: The bridge was built in 1890. They were arrested.

examples.sentence: The Eiffel Tower was built in 1889.
examples.translation: The Eiffel Tower was built in 1889.

examples.sentence: Three people were injured in the accident.
examples.translation: Three people were injured in the accident.

title: Passive Voice - Present Perfect: has/have been + V3
shortExplanation: The car has been repaired. All invitations have been sent.
longExplanation:
Present Perfect Passive: has/have been + V3
Used when the result in the present is important, and not when exactly it happened.
formation: The car has been repaired. All invitations have been sent.

examples.sentence: The project has been completed.
examples.translation: The project is completed.

examples.sentence: All the guests have been informed.
examples.translation: All guests have been notified.

title: Reported Speech - time shift
shortExplanation: "I'm tired." → He said he was tired.
longExplanation:
When translated into indirect speech, the tenses are “shifted” back:
• Present Simple → Past Simple: "I work" → he said he worked
• Past Simple → Past Perfect: "I went" → she said she had gone
• Present Perfect → Past Perfect: "I've seen" → he said he had seen
• will → would; can → could; is → was; am going → was going
formation: "I'm tired." → He said he was tired.

examples.sentence: She said: 'I am leaving.' → She said she was leaving.
examples.translation: She said she was leaving.

examples.sentence: He told me: 'I can't come.' → He told me he couldn't come.
examples.translation: He said he couldn't come.

title: Reported questions - indirect questions
shortExplanation: "Where do you live?" → She asked where I lived.
longExplanation:
In indirect questions:
1. No inversion (word order as in the statement)
2. No auxiliary do/did
3. General questions (Yes/No) → if/whether + subject + verb
formation: "Where do you live?" → She asked where I lived.

examples.sentence: "Where do you work?" → She asked where I worked.
examples.translation: She asked where I worked.

examples.sentence: "Are you married?" → He wanted to know if I was married.
examples.translation: He wanted to know if I was married.

pattern: say vs tell in indirect speech
title: say vs tell in indirect speech
shortExplanation: He said that... / He told me that... - after tell you need a face!
longExplanation:
say - without the required addition: She said she was tired.
tell - ALWAYS with an addition (to whom it is told): She told me she was tired.
❌ He told that he was late. ✓ He said that he was late.
formation: He said that... / He told me that... - after tell you need a face!

examples.sentence: She said she needed help.
examples.translation: She said she needed help.

examples.sentence: He told us the meeting was cancelled.
examples.translation: He informed us that the meeting was cancelled.

title: Verbs + gerund (V-ing)
shortExplanation: I enjoy reading. She finished writing. He avoided making mistakes.
longExplanation:
These verbs require a gerund (V-ing) after them:
enjoy, finish, avoid, mind, suggest, keep, consider, deny, imagine, miss, practice, risk, admit, delay, dislike, fancy, give up, involve, put off, recommend, resist
Memorization trick: if you can replace it with “process”, it’s most likely a gerund.
formation: I enjoy reading. She finished writing. He avoided making mistakes.

examples.sentence: I enjoy swimming in the sea.
examples.translation: I like to swim in the sea.

examples.sentence: She's considering moving abroad.
examples.translation: She is thinking about moving abroad.

examples.sentence: He avoided making eye contact.
examples.translation: He avoided eye contact.

title: Verbs + infinitive (to + V)
shortExplanation: I want to go. She decided to stay. He managed to finish.
longExplanation:
These verbs require an infinitive with to:
want, decide, hope, plan, manage, agree, promise, refuse, fail, expect, offer, learn, need, afford, arrange, attempt, choose, claim, demand, deserve, help, pretend, tend, threaten
formation: I want to go. She decided to stay. He managed to finish.

examples.sentence: She decided to quit her job.
examples.translation: She decided to quit.

examples.sentence: I hope to see you soon.
examples.translation: Hope to see you soon.

examples.sentence: He failed to answer.
examples.translation: He couldn't answer.

pattern: Verbs with both (like, love, hate, start, begin)
title: Verbs with both (like, love, hate, start, begin)
shortExplanation: I like reading = I like to read - slight difference
longExplanation:
After like/love/hate/prefer both options are possible:
• V-ing - we talk about the action as a whole: I love cooking. (I generally like to cook)
• to-inf - we are talking about a specific case: I'd like to cook tonight.
After start/begin/continue/cease there is practically no difference.
formation: I like reading = I like to read - slight difference

examples.sentence: I love travelling / to travel.
examples.translation: I like to travel.

examples.sentence: She started working / to work here in May.
examples.translation: She started working here in May.

title: used to - past habits and states
shortExplanation: I used to play football. She used to have long hair.
longExplanation:
used to - regular actions or conditions in the past that have already stopped.
Form: used to + infinitive
Denial: didn't use to
Question: Did you use to...?
Difference from be used to: I am used to waking up early = I'm used to it (now).
formation: I used to play football. She used to have long hair.

examples.sentence: I used to smoke, but I stopped.
examples.translation: I used to smoke, but I quit.

examples.sentence: Did you use to play an instrument?
examples.translation: Have you played an instrument before?

title: Relative clauses: who, which, that, where, whose
shortExplanation: The man who called. The book that I read. The place where we met.
longExplanation:
who - for people: The woman who called is my sister.
which - for objects and animals: The book which I borrowed was great.
that - for people and objects (in defining clauses): The car that he bought is new.
where - for places: The café where we met is closed.
whose - accessory: The girl whose bag was stolen...
In colloquial speech, a pronoun is often omitted if it is an object: The film (that) I saw...
formation: The man who called. The book that I read. The place where we met.

examples.sentence: The man who lives next door is very friendly.
examples.translation: The man who lives next door is very friendly.

examples.sentence: The hotel where we stayed had a pool.
examples.translation: The hotel we stayed in had a swimming pool.

title: Conjunctions of contrast: although, however, despite, in spite of, whereas
shortExplanation: Although it was raining, we went out. Despite the rain, we went.
longExplanation:
although / even though / though + subordinate clause.
despite / in spite of + noun / gerund (NOT subordinate clause!).
however + new sentence (after period or semicolon).
whereas is a contrast between two facts.
formation: Although it was raining, we went out. Despite the rain, we went.

examples.sentence: Although she was tired, she kept working.
examples.translation: Although she was tired, she continued to work.

examples.sentence: Despite the rain, he cycled to work.
examples.translation: Despite the rain, he rode his bike to work.

examples.sentence: It was expensive. However, it was worth it.
examples.translation: It was expensive. Still, it was worth it.

title: Future Continuous: will be + V-ing
shortExplanation: I'll be working at 9 tomorrow. She'll be flying over the Atlantic.
longExplanation:
Future Continuous = will be + V-ing
Values:
1. An action that will be in progress at a specific moment in the future: At this time tomorrow, I'll be lying on the beach.
2. Planned, expected action in the future (natural course of events): I'll be seeing her tomorrow anyway.
3. Polite questions about plans (no pressure): Will you be coming to the party?
formation: I'll be working at 9 tomorrow. She'll be flying over the Atlantic.

examples.sentence: Don't call at 8 — I'll be having dinner.
examples.translation: Don't call at 8 - I'll have dinner.

examples.sentence: This time next week I'll be sitting on a beach.
examples.translation: This time next week I'll be sitting on the beach.

title: Future Perfect: will have + V3
shortExplanation: By Friday I will have finished the report. By 2030 they will have built the bridge.
longExplanation:
Future Perfect = will have + V3
An action that will be completed before a certain point in the future.
Often used with by (the time), before: By the time you arrive, I will have cooked dinner.
formation: By Friday I will have finished the report. By 2030 they will have built the bridge.

examples.sentence: I'll have finished this book by Sunday.
examples.translation: I will finish reading this book by Sunday.

examples.sentence: By 2050, scientists will have found a cure.
examples.translation: By 2050, scientists will find a cure.

title: Subordinate goals: to, in order to, so that, so as to
shortExplanation: I study hard to pass. She left early so that she could catch the train.
longExplanation:
to / in order to / so as to + infinitive - goal. In order to and so as to are a little more formal.
so that + subject + verb - purpose with another subject or with a modal.
formation: I study hard to pass. She left early so that she could catch the train.

examples.sentence: She studies hard in order to get a scholarship.
examples.translation: She studies hard to get a scholarship.

examples.sentence: He left early so that he could catch the last train.
examples.translation: He left early to catch the last train.

title: Phrasal verbs - basic
shortExplanation: give up, look up, turn off, find out, get on, put off, carry on
longExplanation:
Phrasal verbs = verb + particle (preposition or adverb). The meaning is often idiomatic.
The most frequent:
• give up = give up, give up
• find out = find out, find out
• turn on/off = turn on/off
• look up = look up (in the dictionary/Internet)
• look after = take care
• put off = put off
• carry on = continue
• get on/along = to get along (with someone)
• bring up = to educate; bring up the topic
• come across = stumble upon
formation: give up, look up, turn off, find out, get on, put off, carry on

examples.sentence: I've given up smoking.
examples.translation: I quit smoking.

examples.sentence: Can you look after my cat while I'm away?
examples.translation: Can you look after my cat while I'm away?

examples.sentence: We need to find out what happened.
examples.translation: We need to find out what happened.

title: Past Perfect Simple: had + V3
shortExplanation: By the time she arrived, he had already left.
longExplanation:
Past Perfect - an action that completed before another moment or event in the past.
Form: had + V3 for all faces.
Negation: hadn't + V3
Question: Had + subject + V3?
Typical conjunctions: before, after, when, by the time, already, just, never
formation: By the time she arrived, he had already left.

examples.sentence: When I arrived, she had already left.
examples.translation: When I arrived, she had already left.

examples.sentence: He had never seen snow before that winter.
examples.translation: He had never seen snow before that winter.

title: Past Perfect Continuous: had been + V-ing
shortExplanation: He had been waiting for two hours when she arrived.
longExplanation:
Past Perfect Continuous = had been + V-ing
Emphasis on the duration of an action that occurred before another point in the past.
Often explains a cause or visible result in the past.
formation: He had been waiting for two hours when she arrived.

examples.sentence: She was exhausted — she'd been working all night.
examples.translation: She was exhausted - she had worked all night.

examples.sentence: How long had you been waiting before she arrived?
examples.translation: How long did you wait before she arrived?

title: must have + V3 - confident conclusion about the past
shortExplanation: She must have forgotten. - I'm sure this is the only explanation
longExplanation:
must have + V3 = I'm sure this happened (the only logical explanation).
Confidence scale:
• must have done - almost certainly happened
• should have done - it was expected to happen
• may/might have done - it may have happened
• can't have done - it probably didn't happen
formation: She must have forgotten. - I'm sure this is the only explanation

examples.sentence: You must have been exhausted after that journey.
examples.translation: You must be very tired after this trip.

examples.sentence: She must have left early — her coat is gone.
examples.translation: She apparently left early - her coat was missing.

title: can't have + V3 - impossibility in the past
shortExplanation: She can't have said that! He can't have been there.
longExplanation:
can't have + V3 = I'm sure this didn't happen (it's impossible).
The opposite of must have done.
formation: She can't have said that! He can't have been there.

examples.sentence: He can't have seen her — she was abroad.
examples.translation: He couldn't see her - she was abroad.

examples.sentence: That can't have been the right address.
examples.translation: This could not be the correct address.

title: should have + V3 - reproach and regret
shortExplanation: I should have called. You shouldn't have said that.
longExplanation:
should have + V3 = it would have been right to do it, but I didn’t (regret, reproach).
shouldn't have + V3 = shouldn't have done.
This is a very common construction for expressing regret and criticism.
formation: I should have called. You shouldn't have said that.

examples.sentence: I should have brought an umbrella.
examples.translation: I should have taken an umbrella.

examples.sentence: She shouldn't have told him the secret.
examples.translation: She shouldn't have told him the secret.

title: might / could have + V3 - possibility in the past
shortExplanation: She might have forgotten. It could have been worse.
longExplanation:
might/could have + V3 = this may have happened (we don't know for sure).
Also: could have done = could have done (but didn’t): I could have won if I had tried harder.
formation: She might have forgotten. It could have been worse.

examples.sentence: She might have forgotten about the meeting.
examples.translation: Perhaps she forgot about the meeting.

examples.sentence: He could have left through the back door.
examples.translation: He could have gone out the back door.

title: 3rd type of conditional: If + Past Perfect, would have + V3
shortExplanation: If I had studied harder, I would have passed.
longExplanation:
An unreal situation in the past - we are talking about something that did not happen.
Form: If + Past Perfect, would have + V3
Both elements are unreal:
• Condition not met
• There was no result either
formation: If I had studied harder, I would have passed.

examples.sentence: If she had taken the medicine, she would have recovered.
examples.translation: If she took the medicine, she would get better.

examples.sentence: If he hadn't left early, he would have met her.
examples.translation: If he hadn't left early, he would have met her.

title: Mixed conditionals
shortExplanation: If I had studied, I would be fluent now. (past → present)
longExplanation:
Mixed conditionals connect different time plans:
1. Past condition → present result:
If + Past Perfect, would + infinitive
If I had taken that job, I would be in New York now.
2. Present condition → past result:
If + Past Simple, would have + V3
If she were more careful, she wouldn't have broken it.
formation: If I had studied, I would be fluent now. (past → present)

examples.sentence: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
examples.translation: If I had studied to become a doctor, I would be a doctor now.

pattern: Future Passive and Passive with modals
title: Future Passive and Passive with modals
shortExplanation: It will be done. It must be fixed. It should be checked.
longExplanation:
Modal + Passive: modal + be + V3
• will be done - will be done
• must be done - must be done
• should be done - should be done
• can be done - can be done
formation: It will be done. It must be fixed. It should be checked.

examples.sentence: The report will be published tomorrow.
examples.translation: The report will be published tomorrow.

examples.sentence: This mistake must be corrected immediately.
examples.translation: This error must be corrected immediately.

title: Causative have/get: have something done
shortExplanation: I had my hair cut. She got her car fixed.
longExplanation:
have/get + object + V3 - you order a service or someone does something for you.
Compare:
• I cut my hair. - I cut my hair myself (which is not typical)
• I had my hair cut. - cut by a hairdresser
get is a little more conversational, have is a little more formal.
formation: I had my hair cut. She got her car fixed.

examples.sentence: I need to have my teeth checked.
examples.translation: I need to have my teeth checked by a doctor.

examples.sentence: She had her house painted last spring.
examples.translation: Last spring she painted the house (hiring workers).

title: Passive reporting verbs: It is said that... / He is believed to...
shortExplanation: It is thought that prices will rise. She is known to be honest.
longExplanation:
Two construction options with the verbs say, think, believe, report, know, expect, consider:
1. It + passive + that + subordinate clause: It is believed that...
2. Subject + is + V3 + to-infinitive: She is believed to be...
Used in news and official texts.
formation: It is thought that prices will rise. She is known to be honest.

examples.sentence: It is reported that three people were injured.
examples.translation: Three people were reported injured.

examples.sentence: He is thought to have left the country.
examples.translation: He is believed to have left the country.

title: remember / forget + V-ing vs to-inf - difference in meaning
shortExplanation: I remember locking it (fact of the past) vs Remember to lock it (task)
longExplanation:
remember/forget + V-ing - about a past event that we remember/forgot.
remember/forget + to-inf - about the task: remember to do something in the future.
formation: I remember locking it (fact of the past) vs Remember to lock it (task)

examples.sentence: I remember meeting her at a conference.
examples.translation: I remember meeting her at a conference.

examples.sentence: Remember to call your mother!
examples.translation: Don't forget to call your mom!

examples.sentence: I forgot to buy milk.
examples.translation: I forgot to buy milk.

pattern: stop / regret / mean + V-ing vs to-inf
title: stop / regret / mean + V-ing vs to-inf
shortExplanation: She stopped smoking vs She stopped to smoke
longExplanation:
stop + V-ing - stop the action.
stop + to-inf - stop to do something else.
regret + V-ing - to regret the past.
regret + to-inf - regret to inform you (formally): I regret to inform you...
mean + V-ing - mean: This means working harder.
mean + to-inf - intend: I meant to call you.
formation: She stopped smoking vs She stopped to smoke

examples.sentence: He stopped smoking last year.
examples.translation: He quit smoking last year.

examples.sentence: She stopped to look at the view.
examples.translation: She stopped to admire the view.

title: wish + Past Simple - desire to change the present
shortExplanation: I wish I knew the answer. I wish I had more time.
longExplanation:
wish + Past Simple - about an unrealistic desire in the present.
The form is the same as in the 2nd type of conditional. For to be - were (formally), although was is also used.
formation: I wish I knew the answer. I wish I had more time.

examples.sentence: I wish I spoke better English.
examples.translation: It's a pity that I don't speak English better.

examples.sentence: She wishes she lived in a warmer country.
examples.translation: She would like to live in a warmer country.

title: wish + Past Perfect - regret about the past
shortExplanation: I wish I had studied harder. I wish I hadn't said that.
longExplanation: wish + Past Perfect - regret about past events that cannot be changed. The form is as in the 3rd type of conditional.
formation: I wish I had studied harder. I wish I hadn't said that.

examples.sentence: I wish I hadn't eaten so much.
examples.translation: It's a shame I ate so much.

examples.sentence: She wishes she had taken that job offer.
examples.translation: She wishes she had accepted that job offer.

title: wish + would - desire to change someone else's behavior
shortExplanation: I wish you would stop talking. I wish it would warm up.
longExplanation: wish + would - irritation due to someone else's behavior or a desire to change the situation.
formation: I wish you would stop talking. I wish it would warm up.

examples.sentence: I wish you would listen to me.
examples.translation: I wish you would listen to me.

examples.sentence: I wish it would stop raining.
examples.translation: I wish the rain would stop.

title: Defining vs non-defining clauses
shortExplanation: The man who called (determines which one) vs My brother, who called, (adds info)
longExplanation:
Defining (defining): without commas - they clarify who/what they are talking about. The pronoun can be replaced with that. It cannot be removed without losing the meaning.
Non-defining: with commas - add information without changing the meaning. That cannot be used. Can be removed.
formation: The man who called (determines which one) vs My brother, who called, (adds info)

examples.sentence: The film that I told you about is on tonight.
examples.translation: The movie I told you about is showing tonight.

examples.sentence: My sister, who lives in Paris, is visiting next week.
examples.translation: My sister, who lives in Paris, will arrive next week.

title: Prepositions in relative clauses
shortExplanation: the person I work with / the person with whom I work (formally)
longExplanation:
In colloquial speech, the preposition comes at the end: the house I grew up in.
In written/formal speech, the preposition before which/whom: the house in which I grew up.
After the preposition - only which (for things) and whom (for people). Never that!
formation: the person I work with / the person with whom I work (formally)

examples.sentence: The project I'm working on is fascinating.
examples.translation: The project I'm working on is very interesting.

examples.sentence: The project on which I am working is fascinating.
examples.translation: The project on which I am working is very interesting.

title: Consequence conjunctions: so... that, such... that, therefore, as a result
shortExplanation: It was so cold that we stayed inside. She worked hard; therefore, she passed.
longExplanation:
so + adjective/adverb + that: He spoke so quickly that nobody understood.
such + (a/an) + adjective + noun + that: It was such a long film that I fell asleep.
Connecting words of result (between sentences): therefore, consequently, as a result, hence, thus.
formation: It was so cold that we stayed inside. She worked hard; therefore, she passed.

examples.sentence: It was such a good book that I read it twice.
examples.translation: The book was so good that I read it twice.

examples.sentence: She missed the deadline; consequently, she lost the contract.
examples.translation: She missed the deadline; As a result, she lost her contract.

pattern: be used to / get used to + V-ing
title: be used to / get used to + V-ing - habit (real)
shortExplanation: I'm used to waking up early. She's getting used to the cold.
longExplanation:
be used to + V-ing / noun = to be used to (already used to).
get used to + V-ing / noun = get used to (the process of getting used to).
• I used to live in Paris. - used to live (no longer)
• I am used to living in big cities. - used to living in big cities
formation: I'm used to waking up early. She's getting used to the cold.

examples.sentence: I'm not used to getting up so early.
examples.translation: I'm not used to getting up so early.

examples.sentence: It took time, but she got used to the new system.
examples.translation: It took time, but she got used to the new system.

title: Future in the Past: would / was going to
shortExplanation: She said she would call. He was going to leave.
longExplanation:
Future in the Past - constructions that express the future from the point of view of the past. Used in indirect speech and narrative.
• would + V (from will): She said she would come.
• was/were going to + V: He was going to call but forgot.
• was about to + V: She was about to leave when he arrived.
formation: She said she would call. He was going to leave.

examples.sentence: She promised she would be there.
examples.translation: She promised that she would come.

examples.sentence: He was about to leave when she called.
examples.translation: He was about to leave when she called.

title: be to - official appointment and order
shortExplanation: You are to report by Monday. They were never to meet again.
longExplanation:
be to + infinitive - official orders, planned events and fate in the narrative.
1. Legal Instruction: Passengers are to remain seated.
2. Official plan: The summit is to take place next month.
3. Fate in the narrative: They were never to meet again.
formation: You are to report by Monday. They were never to meet again.

examples.sentence: You are to submit the report by Friday.
examples.translation: You must submit your report by Friday.

examples.sentence: She was to become one of the greatest scientists of her time.
examples.translation: She was destined to become one of the greatest scientists.

title: ought to - moral duty and logical expectation
shortExplanation: You ought to apologise. She ought to have told us.
longExplanation:
ought to is a moral obligation or logical expectation. Stronger should.
Always with to: ought to go (as opposed to should).
For the past: ought to have + V3 - reproach or regret.
formation: You ought to apologise. She ought to have told us.

examples.sentence: You ought to apologise for what you said.
examples.translation: You should apologize for what you said.

examples.sentence: She ought to have told us earlier.
examples.translation: She should have told us sooner.

title: need - modal and regular verb
shortExplanation: You needn't worry. / She doesn't need to come.
longExplanation:
need as a modal (formal, in questions/negations) and as a regular verb.
Modal (without -s, without to):
• You needn't worry. / Need I explain?
Regular need + to:
• She doesn't need to come.
formation: You needn't worry. / She doesn't need to come.

examples.sentence: You needn't fill in both forms.
examples.translation: You do not need to fill out both forms.

examples.sentence: She doesn't need to attend every meeting.
examples.translation: She does not have to attend every meeting.

title: dare - courage and challenge
shortExplanation: How dare you! I daren't ask. She dared to challenge him.
longExplanation:
dare - dare, dare. Modal in rhetorical questions and negations.
Modal: How dare you! / I daren't ask. / Dare I say...
Normal: She didn't dare to look. / He dared to challenge the boss.
formation: How dare you! I daren't ask. She dared to challenge him.

examples.sentence: How dare you speak to me like that!
examples.translation: How dare you talk to me like that!

examples.sentence: She dared to express her opinion openly.
examples.translation: She dared to openly express her opinion.

title: Reflexive pronouns: myself, yourself, himself...
shortExplanation: I hurt myself. She did it herself. They enjoyed themselves.
longExplanation:
myself, yourself, yourself, yourself, yourself, yourself, yourselves, yourself.
1. The action is directed towards the subject: He cut himself.
2. Emphase (by yourself, without help): I did it myself.
Stable: by myself = alone; help yourself = help yourself.
formation: I hurt myself. She did it herself. They enjoyed themselves.

examples.sentence: She taught herself to play the guitar.
examples.translation: She taught herself to play the guitar.

examples.sentence: The machine turns itself off automatically.
examples.translation: The machine turns off automatically.

title: Collective nouns: team, family, committee...
shortExplanation: The team are playing well. (BrE) / The team is playing. (AmE)
longExplanation:
Collective nouns are a group as a whole.
• BrE: usually plural. number: The team are playing.
• AmE: usually units. number: The team is playing.
Frequent: team, family, government, committee, staff, audience, crew, police, army, public, management
formation: The team are playing well. (BrE) / The team is playing. (AmE)

examples.sentence: The government have announced new measures. (BrE)
examples.translation: The government announced new measures.

examples.sentence: The audience were on their feet. (BrE)
examples.translation: The audience jumped to their feet.

title: Fractions and mathematics
shortExplanation: a half, three quarters, 5.7 = five point seven, 25%
longExplanation:
Fractions:½ = a half; ⅓ = a third; ¼ = a quarter; ¾ = three quarters; ⅔ = two thirds.
Numerator is quantitative, denominator is ordinal (plural if numerator > 1).
Decimals: period (not comma): 3.14 = three point one four.
Mathematics: + = plus; - = minus; × = times; ÷ = divided by; = = equals.
formation: a half, three quarters, 5.7 = five point seven, 25%

examples.sentence: Three quarters of students passed the exam.
examples.translation: Three quarters of the students passed the exam.

examples.sentence: The inflation rate fell to 2.5 percent.
examples.translation: The inflation rate dropped to 2.5 percent.

title: Degrees of comparison of adverbs
shortExplanation: faster, more carefully, best, worse, further
longExplanation:
Adverbs form degrees of comparison according to the same rules as adjectives.
• Monosyllabic: + er/est: fast→faster, hard→harder, early→earlier
• Most on -ly: more/most: carefully→more carefully→most carefully
• Incorrect: well→better→best, badly→worse→worst, far→further→furthest, little→less→least, much→more→most
formation: faster, more carefully, best, worse, further

examples.sentence: She spoke more confidently than before.
examples.translation: She spoke more confidently than before.

examples.sentence: He works hardest in the team.
examples.translation: He works harder than anyone on the team.

title: Inversion with negative adverbs
shortExplanation: Never have I seen this. Rarely does she complain.
longExplanation:
For emphasis, the negative adverb/expression is placed at the beginning → auxiliary verb before the subject (word order as in a question).
Words that trigger inversion: never, rarely, rarely, little, hardly, scarcely, barely, not only, only, no sooner
formation: Never have I seen this. Rarely does she complain.

examples.sentence: Never have I seen anything so beautiful.
examples.translation: I have never seen anything so beautiful.

examples.sentence: Rarely does she make a mistake.
examples.translation: She rarely makes mistakes.

examples.sentence: Little did I know what was coming.
examples.translation: I had no idea what was waiting for me.

pattern: Not only... but also with inversion
title: Not only... but also with inversion
shortExplanation: Not only did he apologise, but he also offered to help.
longExplanation:
Not only + inversion in the first part, the second part is the usual order.
Used for emphasis: expresses that something went further than expected.
formation: Not only did he apologise, but he also offered to help.

examples.sentence: Not only is she talented, but she is also very hard-working.
examples.translation: She is not only talented, but also very hardworking.

examples.sentence: Not only did they arrive late, but they also forgot the documents.
examples.translation: They were not only late, but also forgot their documents.

title: Hardly / Scarcely / No sooner + inversion
shortExplanation: Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.
longExplanation:
Immediate sequence constructions:
• Hardly/Scarcely + had + subject + V3 + when/before + Past Simple
• No sooner + had + subject + V3 + than + Past Simple
formation: Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.

examples.sentence: Hardly had she arrived when it started to rain.
examples.translation: She had barely arrived when it started to rain.

examples.sentence: No sooner had I sat down than someone knocked at the door.
examples.translation: I had just sat down when someone knocked on the door.

title: Inversion in conditionals: Had / Were / Should
shortExplanation: Had I known (= If I had known). Were I you (= If I were you).
longExplanation:
Formal style - excludes if, uses inversion:
• Had + subject + V3 = If + Past Perfect (3rd type)
• Were + subject (+ to + infinitive) = If + Past Simple (2nd type)
• Should + subject + infinitive = If (unlikely, type 1)
formation: Had I known (= If I had known). Were I you (= If I were you).

examples.sentence: Had she told me, I would have helped.
examples.translation: If she had told me, I would have helped.

examples.sentence: Were I in your position, I would accept.
examples.translation: If I were you, I would agree.

examples.sentence: Should you need assistance, please call us.
examples.translation: If you need assistance, call us.

title: It-cleft: It was John who called.
shortExplanation: To highlight any member of a sentence
longExplanation:
Structure: It + to be + selected element + who/that/which + rest
Shifts the focus of attention to the highlighted element.
• For people - who; for things/circumstances - that/which.
formation: To highlight any member of a sentence

examples.sentence: It was the noise that woke me up.
examples.translation: It was the noise that woke me up.

examples.sentence: It is hard work that leads to success.
examples.translation: It is hard work that leads to success.

title: Wh-cleft: What surprised me was the price.
shortExplanation: What I need is rest. What she said shocked everyone.
longExplanation:
Structure: What + subordinate clause + to be + highlighted element
Emphasizes the importance of the element introduced at the end.
formation: What I need is rest. What she said shocked everyone.

examples.sentence: What I love about London is the diversity.
examples.translation: What I like most about London is the diversity.

examples.sentence: What he did was completely unexpected.
examples.translation: What he did was completely unexpected.

pattern: Formal subjunctive after verbs of demand
title: Formal subjunctive after verbs of demand
shortExplanation: I suggest he leave. It is vital that she be informed.
longExplanation:
After suggest, recommend, insist, demand, propose, request, require, ask, advise, order + that - the basic form of the verb for all persons (without -s, without was).
The British version often uses should instead of the subjunctive: I suggest that he should leave.
American - often a pure subjunctive.
formation: I suggest he leave. It is vital that she be informed.

examples.sentence: I recommend that he see a doctor.
examples.translation: I recommend that he see a doctor.

examples.sentence: It is essential that all students attend the meeting.
examples.translation: It is essential that all students attend the meeting.

title: It's high time + Past Simple
shortExplanation: It's high time you went to bed. It's time we left.
longExplanation:
It's (high/about) time + subject + Past Simple
Meaning: present/future - we are talking about something that should have been done a long time ago.
high time - even stronger: it’s high time!
formation: It's high time you went to bed. It's time we left.

examples.sentence: It's time she found a new job.
examples.translation: It's high time she found a new job.

examples.sentence: It's high time you apologised.
examples.translation: It's high time to apologize.

title: as if / as though + subjunctive
shortExplanation: She talks as if she knew everything. He looked as though he had seen a ghost.
longExplanation:
as if / as though + Past Simple is an unrealistic comparison in the present.
as if / as though + Past Perfect is an unrealistic comparison about the past.
formation: She talks as if she knew everything. He looked as though he had seen a ghost.

examples.sentence: He spends money as if he were a millionaire.
examples.translation: He spends money like he's a millionaire.

examples.sentence: She spoke as though she had met him before.
examples.translation: She spoke as if she had met him before.

title: So / Neither + auxiliary verb + subject
shortExplanation: So do I. Neither does she. So am I.
longExplanation:
So + auxiliary + subject - agreement with the affirmative.
Neither/Nor + auxiliary + subject - agreement with the negative.
The auxiliary verb must coincide with the tense of the original sentence.
formation: So do I. Neither does she. So am I.

examples.sentence: I love jazz. So does she.
examples.translation: I love jazz. She too.

examples.sentence: I haven't been to Rome. Neither have I.
examples.translation: I haven't been to Rome. Me too.

pattern: I think so / I hope so / I'm afraid so
title: I think so / I hope so / I'm afraid so
shortExplanation: Will it rain? - I think so. / I hope not.
longExplanation:
so replaces the subordinate clause after: think, hope, suppose, expect, believe, imagine, be afraid.
Negative form: not (not so not!).
formation: Will it rain? - I think so. / I hope not.

examples.sentence: Will he come? — I think so. / I don't think so.
examples.translation: Will he come? - I think yes. / Don't think.

examples.sentence: Is it expensive? — I'm afraid so.
examples.translation: Is it expensive? - I'm afraid so.

examples.sentence: Is it closed? — I hope not.
examples.translation: Closed? - I hope not.

title: Inclusive vs non-inclusive clauses
shortExplanation: The man who called is my brother. VS My brother, who called, is a doctor.
longExplanation:
Defining: specifies who/what we are talking about - without commas. that is possible. The pronoun can be omitted if it is an object.
Non-defining: adds information - commas required. Only who/which (not that!). The pronoun cannot be omitted.
formation: The man who called is my brother. VS My brother, who called, is a doctor.

examples.sentence: The film that won the Oscar was brilliant.
examples.translation: The film that won the Oscar was great.

examples.sentence: Avatar, which came out in 2009, was a huge hit.
examples.translation: Avatar, released in 2009, became a big hit.

title: Preposition + which/whom in formal style
shortExplanation: The company for which I work. The person with whom I spoke.
longExplanation:
Formal style: preposition + which/whom before a relative pronoun.
Informal equivalent: preposition at the end of a sentence.
whom is the formal object form of who.
formation: The company for which I work. The person with whom I spoke.

examples.sentence: The report to which I referred is attached.
examples.translation: The report I mentioned is attached.

examples.sentence: The report which I referred to is attached.
examples.translation: The report I mentioned is attached.

examples.sentence: The report I referred to is attached.
examples.translation: The report I mentioned is attached.

title: Nominalization - Basics
shortExplanation: decide→decision, discover→discovery, improve→improvement
longExplanation:
Nominalization is the conversion of verbs/adjectives into nouns. A sign of academic and business style.
Main suffixes:
• -tion/-sion: decide→decision, discuss→discussion
• -ment: improve→improvement, develop→development
• -ance/-ence: appear→appearance, differ→difference
• -ity: complex→complexity, able→ability
• -ness: happy→happiness, aware→awareness
formation: decide→decision, discover→discovery, improve→improvement

examples.sentence: She decided to expand. → Our decision to expand the company...
examples.translation: Our decision to expand...

examples.sentence: He discovered that... → His discovery of the error...
examples.translation: His discovery of the error...

title: Nominalization in academic text
shortExplanation: The fact that prices increased → The increase in prices...
longExplanation:
Nominalization allows:
1. Compress information: There was a significant increase in prices.
2. Add definitions: The rapid increase in house prices...
3. Create a formal, impersonal tone.
formation: The fact that prices increased → The increase in prices...

examples.sentence: There has been a significant improvement in air quality.
examples.translation: Air quality has improved significantly.

examples.sentence: His refusal to comment surprised everyone.
examples.translation: His refusal to comment surprised everyone.

title: Present participle: V-ing clause
shortExplanation: Walking down the street, I saw an old friend. Having no money, he couldn't buy food.
longExplanation:
The participial phrase with Present Participle (V-ing) replaces the subordinate clause:
• Simultaneity: Walking home, I noticed something strange. (= While I was walking home)
• Reason: Knowing the answer, she raised her hand. (= Because she knew)
Error: Walking down the street, the rain started. (the rain did not fall on the street)
formation: Walking down the street, I saw an old friend. Having no money, he couldn't buy food.

examples.sentence: Arriving at the airport, he realised he had forgotten his passport.
examples.translation: Arriving at the airport, he realized that he had forgotten his passport.

examples.sentence: Not knowing what to do, she called her mother.
examples.translation: Not knowing what to do, she called her mother.

title: Past participial phrase: V3 / Having + V3 clause
shortExplanation: Written in 1815, the novel... Having finished work, she went home.
longExplanation:
V3 clause (Past Participle) = passive meaning: Built in 1889, the Eiffel Tower...
Having + V3 = action completed before the main one:
Having read the report, he called a meeting. (= After he had read...)
formation: Written in 1815, the novel... Having finished work, she went home.

examples.sentence: Surprised by the news, she sat down silently.
examples.translation: Surprised by the news, she sat down silently.

examples.sentence: Having finished the exam, the students left the room.
examples.translation: Having finished the exam, the students left the classroom.

pattern: Conditional with unless / provided / as long as / on condition that
title: Conditional with unless / provided / as long as / on condition that
shortExplanation: Unless you study, you'll fail. As long as you're honest, I'll help.
longExplanation:
unless = if not (but cannot be used with negation!): Unless you hurry = If you don't hurry
provided/providing (that) = if and only if (strict condition)
as long as = provided that (assumption)
on condition that = on condition that (formally)
in case = in case
formation: Unless you study, you'll fail. As long as you're honest, I'll help.

examples.sentence: I'll lend you money, as long as you pay me back.
examples.translation: I'll lend you money on the condition that you pay it back.

examples.sentence: You can use my laptop, provided you don't download anything.
examples.translation: You can use my laptop, as long as you don't download anything.

title: Suppose / supposing / what if
shortExplanation: Suppose you won the lottery - what would you do?
longExplanation:
Suppose/Supposing - used as if in hypothetical questions.
What if is an informal analogue.
With Past Simple - a situation is unlikely or imaginary.
formation: Suppose you won the lottery - what would you do?

examples.sentence: Supposing you had to choose — which would you pick?
examples.translation: Imagine that you had to choose - what would you choose?

examples.sentence: What if nobody comes? What should we do?
examples.translation: What if no one comes? What should we do?

title: Only + circumstance + inversion
shortExplanation: Only when I left did I realize. Only then did he understand.
longExplanation:
Only + when/after/if/then/by/in/on - the entire group is moved to the beginning → inversion.
This is one of the most powerful rhetorical devices in writing and public speaking.
formation: Only when I left did I realize. Only then did he understand.

examples.sentence: Only when you experience it can you truly understand.
examples.translation: Only by experiencing it can one truly understand.

examples.sentence: Only after years of practice did she master the skill.
examples.translation: It was only after years of practice that she mastered the skill.

title: So + adjective/adverb + inversion
shortExplanation: So great was his relief that he wept. Such was her talent...
longExplanation:
Book and oratorical style.
So + adj/adv + be/aux + subject
Such + was/were + subject
formation: So great was his relief that he wept. Such was her talent...

examples.sentence: So rapid was the change that nobody could adapt.
examples.translation: The changes happened so quickly that no one could adapt.

examples.sentence: Such was her talent that she was offered a scholarship.
examples.translation: So great was her talent that she was offered a scholarship.

title: Hedging: appear to, seem to, tend to, be likely to
shortExplanation: Prices appear to be rising. This tends to occur when...
longExplanation:
Hedging is the deliberate softening of statements to express scientific modesty.
Main structures:
• appear/seem to - apparently
• tend to - as a rule, tend to
• be likely/unlikely to - likely/unlikely
• be thought/considered to be - it is believed that
formation: Prices appear to be rising. This tends to occur when...

examples.sentence: The results appear to suggest a correlation.
examples.translation: The results appear to indicate a correlation.

examples.sentence: Companies tend to underestimate implementation costs.
examples.translation: Companies tend to underestimate implementation costs.

title: Discourse markers in academic text
shortExplanation: Furthermore, Nevertheless, Conversely, In light of, With regard to
longExplanation:
Markers structure and connect academic text:
• Addition: Moreover, Furthermore, In addition, Additionally
• Contrast: However, nevertheless, nevertheless, Conversely, On the other hand
• Result: Therefore, Consequently, As a result, Hence, Thus
• Explanation: In other words, That is to say, Namely
• Concession: Admittedly, While it is true that, Despite this
formation: Furthermore, Nevertheless, Conversely, In light of, With regard to

examples.sentence: The experiment failed. Nevertheless, the findings were instructive.
examples.translation: The experiment failed. Still, the results were instructive.

examples.sentence: Furthermore, the data suggests a strong correlation.
examples.translation: Moreover, the data suggests a strong correlation.

title: Speech registers: formal, neutral, colloquial
shortExplanation: I would like to enquire... vs I'd like to ask... vs Can I ask...
longExplanation:
Register is determined by purpose, audience and context.
Formal: passive, nominalization, complex conjunctions, full forms, verbs of Latin origin (commence, terminate, assist).
Neutral: standard grammar, no slang, moderate abbreviations.
Informal: ellipsis, phrasal verbs (put off = postpone), contractions, colloquial expressions.
formation: I would like to enquire... vs I'd like to ask... vs Can I ask...

examples.sentence: Formal: I wish to draw your attention to a discrepancy.
Neutral: I want to point out a mistake.
Informal: Just wanted to flag something up.

title: Connotations of synonyms - shades of meaning
shortExplanation: thin/slim/slender/skinny/gaunt: positive→neutral→negative
longExplanation:
Synonyms differ in connotation (emotional coloring) and register.
Examples of scales:
• slim (+) → thin (0) → skinny (-) → scrawny/gaunt (--)
• determined (+) → firm (0) → stubborn/pig-headed (-)
• thrifty (+) → economical (0) → stingy/tight-fisted (-)
• confident (+) → assertive (0) → arrogant (-)
formation: thin/slim/slender/skinny/gaunt: positive→neutral→negative

examples.sentence: She is slim. (+) / She is thin. (0) / She is skinny. (-)
examples.translation: Same thing, but different attitude.

title: Rhetorical devices: anaphora, chiasmus, tricolon
shortExplanation: "We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds..." - anaphora
longExplanation:
Anaphora: repetition of words at the beginning of successive sentences. "I have a dream... I have a dream..."
Chiasmus: AB-BA cross structure. "Ask not what your country can do for you, but what you can do for your country."
Tricolon: three parallel elements. "Veni, vidi, vici." / "Government of the people, by the people, for the people."
These techniques are used in oratory, essays and journalism.
formation: "We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds..." - anaphora

examples.sentence: Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears.
examples.translation: Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears.

examples.sentence: The more you learn, the more you earn.
examples.translation: The more you learn, the more you earn.

title: Precise collocations in academic text
shortExplanation: conduct research, draw conclusions, reach a consensus, address an issue
longExplanation:
In C2 it is important to use the 'correct' verb with each noun.
Academic collocations:
• conduct/carry out research (not make/do)
• draw/reach a conclusion
• raise/address/tackle an issue
• reach/achieve a consensus
• make significant progress
• pose/present a challenge
formation: conduct research, draw conclusions, reach a consensus, address an issue

examples.sentence: Researchers conducted extensive interviews.
examples.translation: The researchers conducted extensive interviews.

examples.sentence: The committee failed to reach a consensus.
examples.translation: The committee was unable to reach consensus.

title: Absolute construction with participle
shortExplanation: Weather permitting, we'll have a picnic. Her eyes filled with tears, she left the room.
longExplanation:
Absolute construction = noun/pronoun + participle (independent subject).
Used in written and formal style - adds a circumstance without a conjunction.
Types:
• Weather permitting = If the weather permits
• All things considered = If you consider everything
• Her work finished = When/After her work was finished
• This done = When/After this was done
formation: Weather permitting, we'll have a picnic. Her eyes filled with tears, she left the room.

examples.sentence: All things considered, it was a successful event.
examples.translation: All things considered, it was a successful event.

examples.sentence: The deadline having passed, the project was cancelled.
examples.translation: After the deadline passed, the project was cancelled.

pattern: Ellipsis and substitution in connected text
title: Ellipsis and substitution in connected text
shortExplanation: I wanted to go but didn't (want to). She said she'd call and she did.
longExplanation:
Ellipsis is the omission of already known elements.
Substitution - using do/so/one/it instead of repeating.
Ellipse types:
• A: Are you coming? B: Might (do).
• She speaks French and he does too / so does he.
• I wanted to leave, but wasn't allowed to. (leave omitted)
Substitution: I thought he'd pass. He did. / The big one? I prefer the small one
formation: I wanted to go but didn't (want to). She said she'd call and she did.

examples.sentence: Can you drive? — I used to (drive).
examples.translation: Can you drive? - I used to be able to.

examples.sentence: She said she'd be here and she was.
examples.translation: She said she would come, and she came.

pattern: Infinitive phrases instead of subordinate clauses
title: Infinitive phrases instead of subordinate clauses
shortExplanation: I want you to explain. She asked me to help. He doesn't seem to be happy.
longExplanation:
Complex infinitive (Complex Object) replaces the subordinate clause:
I want + object + to-infinitive: I want her to stay.
After see, hear, watch, let, make, have - infinitive without to:
I saw her leave. / She made him cry. / Let me help.
In the passive - with to: He was made to pay.
Constructions with seem, appear, happen, prove + to-inf:
She seems to know. / He happened to be there.
formation: I want you to explain. She asked me to help. He doesn't seem to be happy.

examples.sentence: I need you to sign this document.
examples.translation: I need you to sign this document.

examples.sentence: She was made to apologise publicly.
examples.translation: She was forced to publicly apologize.

examples.sentence: He seemed to have forgotten everything.
examples.translation: He seemed to have forgotten everything.

title: Future Perfect Continuous: will have been + V-ing
shortExplanation: By next year, I will have been studying English for five years.
longExplanation:
Future Perfect Continuous = will have been + V-ing
Emphasis on the duration of an action that will last until a certain point in the future. Often answers the question “How long by then?”
Often used with by (the time), for, when: By Monday, she will have been working on this project for three weeks.
formation: By next year, I will have been studying English for five years.

examples.sentence: By next year, I will have been learning English for five years.
examples.translation: By next year I will have been studying English for five years.

examples.sentence: When we arrive, she will have been waiting for two hours.
examples.translation: When we arrive, she will already have been waiting for two hours.

title: Coordination of tenses - sequence of tenses
shortExplanation: She said she had been working. He thought it would be difficult.
longExplanation:
In complex sentences, the verb of the subordinate clause agrees in time with the main one.
If the main verb is in the past:
• Present Simple → Past Simple: he said it was true
• Past Simple → Past Perfect: she said she had seen it
• Present Perfect → Past Perfect: he said he had finished
• will → would; can → could; may → might; is → was
formation: She said she had been working. He thought it would be difficult.

examples.sentence: He told me that he had been living there for years.
examples.translation: He told me that he had lived there for many years.

examples.sentence: She said the Earth moves around the Sun.
examples.translation: She said that the Earth moves around the Sun.

title: Coordinating conjunctions: and, but, or, nor, for, yet, so
shortExplanation: FANBOYS: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So
longExplanation:
Coordinating conjunctions connect equivalent parts of a sentence.
Seven Basic (acronym FANBOYS):
• for = because (formal): She left, for she was tired.
• and = and (adding)
• nor = and not (Neither/Nor... inversion!): She didn't call, nor did she write.
• but = but (contrast)
• or = or (alternative)
• yet = however (contrast, more formal but)
• so = therefore (consequence)
formation: FANBOYS: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So

examples.sentence: She was tired, yet she kept working.
examples.translation: She was tired, but continued to work.

examples.sentence: He didn't study, nor did he attend class.
examples.translation: He didn't study or go to classes.

title: Subordinating conjunctions: although, whereas, provided, unless...
shortExplanation: although, as though, whereas, provided that, unless, given that, in case
longExplanation:
Subordinating conjunctions introduce subordinate clauses.
By value:
• Time: when, while, as, after, before, until, once, as soon as, whenever
• Reasons: because, since, as, given that, seeing that
• Conditions: if, unless, provided, as long as, in case, supposing
• Goals: so that, in order that, best
• Concessions: although, even though, whereas, while, however
formation: although, as though, whereas, provided that, unless, given that, in case

examples.sentence: Seeing that the deadline had passed, we cancelled the meeting.
examples.translation: Since the deadline passed, we canceled the meeting.

examples.sentence: Lest she forget, he sent her a reminder.
examples.translation: So that she wouldn't forget, he sent her a reminder.

title: Comma, semicolon and colon
shortExplanation: Use a comma before FANBOYS. Use a semicolon to link related clauses.
longExplanation:
Comma:
• Before coordinating conjunctions FANBOYS between independent clauses.
• After introductory words/turns of phrase: However, she decided to stay.
• In the enumerations (Oxford comma - before the last and): apples, oranges, and bananas.
Semicolon (;): connects two independent clauses without a conjunction.
She was tired; she went to bed
Colon (:): introduces a list, explanation, quotation.
formation: Use a comma before FANBOYS. Use a semicolon to link related clauses.

examples.sentence: However, the results were inconclusive; further research is required.
examples.translation: However, the results are mixed; further research is required.

examples.sentence: The company has three priorities: efficiency, innovation, and sustainability.
examples.translation: The company has three priorities: efficiency, innovation and sustainability.

title: Dash, apostrophe and quotation marks
shortExplanation: Em dash - for emphasis - sets off a phrase. It's vs its. "Direct speech"
longExplanation:
Dash (—): highlights a plug-in construction (stronger than a comma): The solution - though expensive - proven effective.
Apostrophe:
• Abbreviations: it's = it is; don't; they're
• Possessive case: John's book; the students' results
• 
Quotes: AmE - double ("text"), BrE - single ('text').
formation: Em dash - for emphasis - sets off a phrase. It's vs its. "Direct speech"

examples.sentence: The project — launched in 2020 — exceeded all expectations.
examples.translation: The project, launched in 2020, exceeded all expectations.

examples.sentence: It's important to check its settings before use.
examples.translation: It is important to check its settings before using it.

pattern: Special and indirect questions in academic text
title: Special and indirect questions in academic text
shortExplanation: The question is whether... / I wonder what the data shows.
longExplanation:
In academic texts, direct questions are replaced by indirect ones (interrogative clauses).
An indirect question is a subordinate clause with the usual word order (without inversion, without do).
Introductory words: whether, if (yes/no), what, where, when, how, why, which.
Example: What does this data show? → The question is what this data shows.
formation: The question is whether... / I wonder what the data shows.

examples.sentence: I wonder whether the hypothesis is correct.
examples.translation: I wonder if the hypothesis is true.

examples.sentence: The study examines how social media affects behaviour.
examples.translation: The study examines how social media influences behavior.
